newsitem.title: USA: Wall Street seen heading upward, HP to drag techs.
newsitem.headline: Wall Street seen heading upward, HP to drag techs.

text.p: Wall Street is seen opening higher Friday, continuing yesterday's late rally despite a possible drag on technology stocks from Hewlett-Packard Co's lower-than-expected earnings.
Analysts see an upward move by stocks as long as housing starts data, due at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT, are in line with expectations.
On Thursday a late rally pushed the Dow to a new high of 7334, up about 47 points on the day.

"If the economic numbers are supportive...I think we will be headed to a higher market with a little volatily because of the double options" expirations, said Peter Cardillo, director of research at Westfalia Investments.
Friday sees "double witching" expirations of individual and index options, which often leads to swings in the stock market.

Analysts said Hewlett-Packard is expected to weigh down the high-technology sector. The company posted fiscal second quarter earnings of $0.75 per share, below the First Call consensus estimate of $0.80.
"Hewlett-Packard could be a drag today because of its earnings report," said Thom Brown, managing director of Rutherford Brown and Catherwood.
Brown does not expect housing starts to have a big effect on the market. April starts are expected to come in at an annual rate of 1.43 million, against 1.425 million in March.
"I think the market yesterday was fairly impressive based on the strength of the bonds, and that should carry through today," Brown said.
Tokyo's 225-share Nikkei average gained 268.42 points, or 1.34 percent, to 20,324.73.
In London the FTSE 100 was up 15.9 points at 4697.1. U.S. stocks were mixed to lower, unsettled by a weak technology sector.
The dollar was up against the yen in Tokyo and was at 1.6988/98 against the mark in Europe.
The U.S. Treasury 30-year bond was up 1/32 to yield 6.86 percent, and the Standard & Poors 500 futures index was up 0.75 to 845.50.

The Wall Street Journal's Heard on the Street column said a recent study shows small investors are not as bad as people think at picking stocks -- they may be worse, selling winners too soon and buying losers too often.

The New York Times's Market Place column said two investors from New Jersey are the first publicly named targets of a federal probe into possible insider trading of Lotus Development shares before Lotus was purchased by International Business Machines Corp in 1995. The two men have been charged with perjury, the paper said.
